A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same pFedMMA work and provide readable text, equations, figures, and tables. V1 ends after the references despite mentioning an appendix; v2 supplies Appendices A–E. The supplied material supports a reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification experiments under federated data heterogeneity, including benchmark accuracies in Tables 1–3 and learning curves in Figure 2.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark results, ablations, sensitivity experiments, learning curves, and resource measurements in Section 4 and Appendices D–E.

M1.justification: Both versions train modality-specific up/down projections locally and aggregate only the shared cross-modal projection, using the same adapter architecture and cross-entropy objective. V2 combines equivalent equations and adds Algorithm 1; these document the existing procedure rather than introduce a new method.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same eleven datasets: seven CLIP recognition benchmarks, CIFAR-10/100, DomainNet, and Office-Caltech10. OxfordPets already appears in v1 Table 1 despite its omission from the dataset description. Added shots, backbones, and partitions vary settings within retained tasks and domains.

E2.justification: The primary benchmark comparator sets remain unchanged. V2 adds evaluated all-global, reversed-sharing, and local-only adapter controls in Tables 5, 13, and 18. Zero-shot CLIP, included in v1 Figure 2, is omitted from the updated learning-curve comparisons in v2 Figures 4–5.

E3.justification: V2 adds systematic 1/2/4/8/16-shot evaluations, Dirichlet concentration sweeps, and one-versus-two-client domain partitions. ViT-B/32 replaces ResNet50 as the stated alternative backbone and receives reported evaluations. The main domain comparison changes from beta=0.3 to 0.5, while retaining the earlier setting in the appendix. New experiments also vary adapter configurations and report relative-improvement and resource metrics.

E4.justification: V1 lacks direct adapter-design ablations. V2 tests adapter width, scaling, insertion depth, alternative sharing arrangements, and removal of federation in Tables 5 and 11–15 and Table 18. It also adds systematic backbone and heterogeneity analyses, expands convergence analysis across shots and datasets, and examines computational and communication costs.

E5.justification: V1 explicitly reports three-seed averaging for Table 1; v2 Appendix C.2 states that every experiment is repeated with three different seeds. This broadens the disclosed run information without establishing an increase in runs. Neither version reports run dispersion, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces pFedMMA's average HM of 82.85 with 84.15 and PromptFL's 82.15 with 83.09; v1's unspecified shot count prevents treating these as controlled same-setting gains. At beta=0.3, CIFAR-10 entries change from 96.79 to 96.92 for pFedMMA and 92.11 to 93.19 for FedPGP. V2 adds extensive shot, backbone, ablation, and resource results. V1's per-domain beta=0.3 scores are retained in v2 Table 10.

T1.justification: Appendix E.1 adds analytical parameter and communication counts, including m[2r(d_v+d_t)+r^2] trainable parameters and m r^2 parameters uploaded or downloaded per round for pFedMMA. Existing mathematical objectives and update equations remain equivalent. No new convergence or generalization theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: adapter-based personalized federated adaptation of VLMs, balancing personalization and generalization through selective sharing, and reduced communication. The additional experiments support these existing claims without materially redefining their scope.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive interpretations absent from v1: limited few-shot data motivates adapting the last three layers, width 32 balances performance against parameter cost, and inappropriate scaling impairs adaptation or generalization. Appendix E interprets the shared subspace as essential for cross-client coordination and discusses accuracy, computation, and communication tradeoffs.

D1.justification: Appendices A, C, and E add pseudocode, dataset sizes, the equal base/novel class split, ten-class domain subsets, client averaging, PyTorch and NVIDIA A6000 hardware, layer choices, and resource accounting. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation; newly disclosed settings do not establish changes to earlier experiments. Conversely, v1's code-availability statement and repository URL are absent from v2.

R1.justification: V2 adds the OxfordPets reference, Parkhi et al.'s Cats and Dogs, and removes the citation to Ghiasvand et al.'s Decentralized Low-Rank Fine-Tuning of Large Language Models. The substantive related-work discussion and positioning against prompt learning and existing adapters remain largely unchanged; moving that discussion to Appendix B is structural.

P1.justification: V2 moves the entire Related Work section to Appendix B, compresses displayed equations and bullet lists into inline prose, and reorganizes the experimental narrative into performance, ablation, and learning-curve sections. The appendix structure substantially changes how the paper presents its argument, although much existing prose is retained.

P2.justification: V2 adds radar charts, shot-comparison plots, ablation tables, and resource tables. The four-panel learning-curve figure becomes a dataset-by-shot grid with separate averages. Existing tables are redesigned with shaded rows, colored relative-improvement entries, and separate domain-dataset averages. The architecture overview is retained as Figure 2, within a substantially reformatted document.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important gaps in v1 by directly testing the selective-sharing design (Tables 5, 13, and 18), quantifying its previously asserted efficiency (Table 17), and supplying substantial reproducibility details. These additions strengthen the justification for the central method beyond benchmark comparisons. Benefits outweigh the removed code-access statement and remaining overstatements: for example, Table 4 shows one-shot ViT-B/32 HM below FedPGP despite the claim of superiority across all settings.
